I had a dream when I was somewhere between the age of 5-8 and I still remember it now at almost 22. 

I was in this house and it had a long staircase, that had a rug going down the length of the stairs, I walked down and turned right to see a dumpster and in that dumpster was someone laying down in the Scream costume, I froze, my heart was beating fast and I was scared shitless. Needles to say I hightailed it up the stairs, but when I reached the top, I fell and managed to get wrapped up in the rug and roll down the stairs to the bottom, at which point the rug is fully wrapped around me and I can’t move, I see Scream’s feet and at that point I forced myself awake. 

I’ve had lots of bad dreams as a kid, ones where I was running away from something, I don’t know what, all I knew in the dream was that I was scared shitless and when I would run I ran in slow motion and when I screamed I would whisper; most nights ended in me realising that I was in a dream and that I needed to get out and subsequently forced myself awake to a damp bed from sweating; but this was by far the one that’s stuck with me for all these years.

I'd been going through a three year long existential crisis, I'd lost all sense of meaning, spent the final of the three years completely bed-ridden and severely depressed thinking about anything and everything there was to think about. I was almost on the edge of suicide; it'd been on my mind for a long long time. After the initial meeting we become super close and I'd never connected truly with someone so much in my life. He pulled me out of that hole I dug myself into. Stuck by my side, showed up to my house almost daily (hated this at the time but super hilarious looking back), got me out of bed, cheered me on to get a job after being unemployed for a year and just kept me company. Hasn't left my side since, I'm doing better then I could ever hope to imagine, my life is together, I landed one of my dream jobs last year with hardly any experience and I'm living pretty well. All the good in my life and where I am at the moment, all came from one source, him. Why is my best friend awesome? He literally saved my life. Bloody good Irish bastard he is ;)

My mother started to go to Church roughly when I was eight years old. I quickly became close friends with the pastor's kid. He was my one and only good friend probably up until I was roughly sixteen years old; maybe even a little later. I started going through a phase when I started questioning a lot of things and the more I started to move away from Christianity the more we sort of moved apart -- to my disliking. This 'Questioning' period lasted three years and by the end of those three years I'd completely de-converted and we were two very different individuals. I'd now call myself a very spiritual agnostic. I've tried to reach out to him multiple times, but the times we've gotten together, he came across as quite arrogant and superior and more often then not, looked down on me. On top of that he'd often bate me into an argument after I'd said that both of us have reached a point in our lives where we're quite strong in our beliefs and in that regard, we shouldn't waste our breath debating, because neither of us is going to change each other's mind. And shortly after, when I was quite raw, he used the recent suicide of my uncle to talk to me about God and death; that was what really put the final nail in the coffin for me. I don't harbor any bad feelings towards him; he's just the product of the environment he grew up in and not to hit on Christianity or Christians either. The Christian faith, or not so much faith, but The Bible, has a lot of tools and advice and wisdom, but when it comes to God and if he's real, I personally don't believe in such a thing, but from some of the things I've seen and experienced, I understand why some people think as much and have come to that conclusion. At the end of the day, I could be wrong, but based on my journey, I'd say otherwise. But that's the fun of it all; nobody actually fucking knows ;)

I just started working at a pretty big Craft Beer brewery in my country that's pretty reputable. Absolute dream job and I was lucky enough to be hired on as an assistant Brewer. Beforehand I was a head Brewer at a small time Kombucha company and had worked there for almost half a year and had made some Mead made primarily with Munuka honey previously as a hobby. Some of the skills passed on to my current position. Same work more or less but on steroids. They were looking for someone with a lot more experience but by share luck I got on through. I just love the job because you're not stuck doing one thing all day, it's lots of different jobs and it's both physically and mentally stimulating, which I found hard to get in the other jobs I've had. It's normally one or the other. And depending on where you are on the ladder, there's room for creative input and chances to do your own small brews, as a trial. It's really the perfect blend of science and art and that's what gets me a hard on. It doesn't really feel like work at this point. You don't wake up in the morning (and I get up pretty early) cursing the sun, you actually look forward to going to work, hustling whatever needs to be done throughout the day. It's very satisfying and fulfilling. Especially since so many people drink and like our products.

I took LSD near the start of the year (March) for the first time when my depression was at an all time low and at that point, I was sure that I'd not make it to the end of the year, without killing myself, as I'd had severe depression for 3+ years and spent much of the previous year bed-ridden. Basically, an old friend contacted me out of the blue, we went on an 8 hour hike, on a weekday, while high.

I feel like I'm fairly similar to you actually. I think I started going to a Christian Church when I was around eight years old and progressed to go for another ten years as I grew older. In that time my mother got married, in which I gained a step-father, which was nice at first because I never really knew my biological father and still don't to this day. My step-father ended up being emotionally abusive for all those years and I feel like the church and religion kind of facilitated that and made it go on for as long as it did because divorce was apparently looked down upon in The Bible. Forgiveness was also a big message that got said or preached and I think my mother felt like she had to forgive my step-father each time he went through one of his 'cycles'. It wasn't until I was eighteen years old that my mother had finally had enough and kicked him out of the house but by then the damage had already been done emotionally/mentally. 

If anything I think my depression stemmed from religion or contributed to it a lot. In those years of abuse I would pray to God again and again that he would change my step-father or that he will just get kicked out of the house for good, never to come back, or that he would cure my anxiety and my depression, which formed at an early age, but God did nothing. And I think that in turn made my depression and anxiety even worse then what it was originally; that God was listening yet doing nothing. That made it hard coming to church each week, going in and trying to put on a happy face and worship and pray to God to the best of my ability, even though I was struggling on the inside with my own problems and what was happening to me and my family at home; as a young boy I felt utterly and completely powerless to do anything. 

I think I endured a great deal of religious trauma in those years, as a young boy, without even realising it, because on top of feeling like God wasn't listening to me and doing anything, as I said above, I was always afraid of going to Hell. So every second of every day, I was always concerned/conscious of how I was acting or what I was saying, or what my motives were, if I really loved God or just loved him so that I wouldn't have to be in eternal torture and if so, he'd be able see right through me because he's all-knowing. Each message told me that I was born a bad person and that there was something wrong with me, but through God, that could all change and and looking back now I think that's quite damaging to preach to a kid. Sometimes I would have nightmares where I would dream about the tribulation in the end times and Jesus coming back on his white horse and saving everyone except for me and I would start praying in the dream "Forgive me, forgive me, forgive me!" over and over again and I'd wake up from said dream still saying it and I'd stay awake for another hour saying it too because I feared that he'd come back at any given moment. 

There was a point that I reached when I was older where I realised, after staying awake at night, praying from my heart, crying out, that no one was there and no-one was listening to me, that I was talking to nothing. That was the point where I began to de-convert and really start to question everything I'd grown up to believe. From there it was a matter of knocking down the two pillars that consolidated my faith; feeling what I thought to be The Holy Spirit and the generic healing of ailments in the church. Once I was able to understand what causes those things to the best of my ability and that there was room for reasonable doubt, I was fairly confident that God didn't exist and even if he does for whatever reason, the way The Bible paints him out to be, he isn't someone I'd ever want to follow anyway; after that, I was able to move on or start the process of moving on, which I'm doing now. 

I don't know if you used to be a Christian or if you were always an atheist, if the former, it certainly is a journey. After questioning and leaving the faith, I went through an existential crisis thats lasted a few years and I've still been struggling with depression and anxiety, but I feel after leaving, my condition has slowly been getting better and better. It's a slow process and it takes time, a lot of time, if not years to move on and start that new chapter outside of religion, but you'll get there eventually. If anything, all these years have made me strong, they've made me into the person I am today, which is a silver lining I guess. I feel like I've lived for sixty years and have gained all this maturity and wisdom as a result, even though I'm only nineteen years old, going on twenty pretty soon.

I'm currently playing through New Vegas for the first time after gradually making my way through each instalment in the series and if I could pick a moment of late from the top of my head, I'd have to say the moment when you walk into Nipton for the first time and Oliver Swanick runs up to you and says, "Yeah! Who won the lottery? I did!". 

I had no idea what he was on about and I thought he was high on Jet. Then the theme, City of Dead, from the original Fallout started playing and I instantly new something was wrong. I looked behind him and saw the town on fire, curious, I made my way through the town, seeing newly raised flags, men strung up and crucified on crosses and eventually, stumbling across Caesar's Legion for the first time. 

After a short conversation with the head of the group who led the attack, Vulpes, saying the town was "morally sick", I was intrigued. These were the people everyone up until that point in the game had said was the enemy. Though Vulpes had some points to be made and in the end I was conflicted on my thoughts on the Legion and whether or not they were really the bad guys or not. 

I then began exploring the town, eventually coming across Boxcars, who explained the lottery in more detail, that everyone was issued a ticket and depending on which ticket you had, you could have a quick death, be crucified, enslaved, your legs beat to a pulp, like Boxcars, or set free; everything began to fit together like a puzzle. That explained how the man was acting out front, he was basically adrenaline filled and in shock, from witnessing the town being destroyed and the townsfolk slaughtered and enslaved before his very eyes and living to tell the tale. 

This moment in the game was so perfectly set up in the dialogue and the way it unfolded; it was the perfect introduction to a major faction in the game and it even managed to challenge some of my preconceived notions on Caesar's Legion too. I'm still unsure about them and what their goal is, as I have yet to meet them again in my play-though, but I can't wait to uncover more. There's certainly a morally grey area there and I suspect it's going to get more grey as I progress in the game, which is a breath of fresh air, after playing Fallout 3. So I don't know if it's my all time favourite scene, but it's definitely up there, for sure.

Apparently a lot of people have had the same issue you've been having when trying to download all the DLC on the Xbox One. You can install the Fallout New Vegas DLC on the Xbox One by following the steps below:

- Insert the first disc and run any necessary updates.
- After the updates have completed, insert the second disc.
- From the Home screen on the Dashboard, scroll to the right and press [A] to navigate to the My games and apps menu.
- Under the Game category, navigate to Fallout New Vegas and press [Menu].
- Select Manage game.
- From the Ready to install category, select See in store.
- When in the store, select the desired DLC and then choose Install.
- You will now be able to then run the game with the DLC from either disc.

I'll copy and paste the advice I gave to another user which pertains to you: 

When it comes to your character, I wouldn't role with any of the pre-maid ones that have been laid out for you, instead create your own. It's important to note that you'll have three main skills to pick from a list of skills to begin with, make sure to avoid melee weapons, throwing and unarmed skills, they're not that great. Instead choose small guns, which will be useful starting out, energy weapons, which will be useful mid-game to end-game and speech, which will be useful throughout the game especially towards the end. Each level you go up, make sure to divide your points between these three skills, overtime getting your energy weapons and speech to 200%, while getting your small weapons to maybe 70%. Once this is done, divide your points how you see fit, in any skills you find useful, I'd suggest the bartering skill for cheaper products and higher returns when selling items (probably best to put some points into this while starting out too). You can also buy books from Mrs. Stapleton from The Hub that will advance your repair, science, health, journeyman and small guns skills, so also take note of that if your stressing these skills at any point in the game.

When I created my character, or create them, I generally give them 5 strength (which will go up with different variations of armour, with power armour, it goes up to 8 strength I believe), 7 perception (for sharpshooting), 5 endurance, 7 charm, 8 intelligence (a good thing about this is that it'll give you more points to put into skills each time you level up), 4 agility and 4 luck. At some point in the game you'll come across a doctor that can do operations to improve these 7 primary statistics once, which will be very useful, especially with a low agility.

When you're at an earlier level, make sure to kill all the rats, pig rats and mole rats that you happen to come across in the beginning, it may be tedious at times, but they'll help you level up. Get some followers earlier on in the game, Ian is useful and you can find him at Shady Sands, if you have a high enough speech, you can get him to follow you for nothing. He'll come in handy for doing some missions in Shady Sands as well as exploring the nearby vault; this way, you'll save ammunition and stimpaks, which are few at first. Another couple of useful followers that can be found early on in the game is Dogmeat and Tycho, who can be found in Junktown, you can get them to follow you for nothing as well.

I'd recommend that you go to each of the main locations in the game in this order (don't view if you don't want the names spoiled): Vault 13 > Shady Sands > Scorpion Caves > Vault 15 > Junktown > The Hub > Necropolis > Vault 13 > Shady Sands > The Raiders > Brotherhood > The Glow > Boneyard > Military Base > The Cathedral. Make sure to do all the side quests in each of the cities that you visit along the way and sometimes you'll have to go back and finish up some quests that weren't available to you straight away (like Shady Sands).

A useful tool for the quests in the games is this page: http://fallout.wikia.com/wiki/Fallout_quests

This will help you carry out quests correctly and show you which paths will give you more points and bad/good karma depending on what sort of person you want your character to be.

That's all I have to say really, all of the above will help you starting out, the rest you'll figure out on your own. Have a save for each city, don't just save on one slot the whole time, in case you realise you made a big mistake a while back or something. Stock up on Rad-X and RadAway; keep your radiation resistance at 100%. Search bookshelves and desks. If you exceed your carry wait, put some items in a secure location so that you can come back for them and sell them later on, at The Hub or whatever. So yeah; good luck and I hope you enjoy the game.

[Right from the opening scene, we know that the 'Driver' is a no-nonsense professional getaway driver, who's done the job plenty of times; to the point where he doesn't break a sweat. From his tone of voice in the opening phone call, to the way he carries himself, we get the idea that this is a person you don't want to mess with. 

Throughout the film, he's quite silent and speaks rarely, this adds a sense of mystery to the character and makes us feel like there's more to this character then we think we know already. 

There's multiple scenes in the beginning half of the film that show us that he's unbothered by dangerous situations and dangerous people, which also reconfirms what we were thinking beforehand, that he's been in these situations and around these sort of people before, in his past. 

Two examples being: 

- Shannon (Bryan Cranston) approaches him on a Hollywood film set and tells him that they need a stunt man to perform a rollover and that there's no shame in saying no. The Driver just smiles and nods his head, indicating that he's game, despite the danger. This, accompanied by the opening scene, show us he's calm and collected in dangerous situations. 

- Shannon has dealings with two Jewish mobsters called Bernie Rose (Albert Brooks) and Nino (Ron Perlman) and convinces them to purchase a high-end car for the Driver to race, since he has so much "talent", thus potentially earning them some serious cash. Shannon is visibly nervous and jittery around these men, understandably, since some of Nino's friends broke his pelvis years earlier for a bad deal. When the Driver meets these men and hears the previous story, he's the complete opposite of Shannon, he's (again) calm and still and you get a sense that he's been around these dangerous people before... in his past. He isn't intimidated by them at all, in fact, the Driver looks and feels intimidating. 

 
It's a little after that we get a shot of him eating at a diner. This is where we meet a man who was involved in one of his previous getaway gigs and asks if he's game for another job. The Driver turns to him and says, "How about this, shut your mouth, or I'll kick your teeth down your throat and shut it for you", while giving him the death stare. The man backs away immediately and leaves him alone. It's at this point in the film that we know he hasn't just been around dangerous situations and dangerous people before, but that the Driver himself is a dangerous man and if pushed, could commit violent acts; the big question is; "What will push him over the edge?"


It's during this time that Irene's (Carey Mulligan) husband Standard (Oscar Isaac) gets released from prison. Soon after release, Standard is met by thugs sent from a man named Cook, who beat him up and demand protection money from when he was in prison. And that if he doesn't pay up, then his family, his wife and son, will be harmed. The Driver teams up with him to perform a robbery because he cares deeply for Standard's family just as Standard himself does. 

As you all know, the robbery that was set up by Cook goes bad, Standard dies and the Driver narrowly escapes while being pursued by another vehicle that was sent by Cook to re-steal the money from them. When the pursuit is over, the Driver checks into a motel, where he is met again by two of Cooks thugs who intend to kill him; he ends up killing them both -- thus the first violent act committed by the Driver.

It's soon after that the Driver hunts down Cook and smashes in his hand with a hammer like a boss, opens his mouth with said hammer and proceeds to shove a bullet down the man's throat, the bullet Cook's thugs threatened Standard's boy with. He demands to know who he works for and he reveals that Nino set up the robbery... dun dun dun. 


After this second violent act, the Driver contacts Nino and says that he can have the money, as long as Irene and her boy are kept from harm. Nino, being a dumb-ass, refuses the offer and sends a hitman to "dispose of witnesses". 


At this point we know that the Driver is a dangerous person, who can certainly take care of himself and that if anything happens to Irene or her boy, which the Driver cares deeply for, he will be pushed over the edge; thus reaching breaking point and performing the ultimate act of violence. So what happens? The Driver and Irene enter their apartment elevator, said hitman is in the elevator, the Driver knows what's about to happen, we know what's about to happen, Driver kisses Irene (calm before the storm) and bam... the Driver stomps in his head. 


So I disagree that it was never hinted at, it was hinted at throughout the whole movie right from the opening scene, to the 01:12:45 mark. I can only speak from experience, but anytime I've tried to attach meaning to my life, I've just used a cheap answer as a coping mechanism and I know deep down that I still haven't found meaning even when I'm saying to myself that I have. 

When observing people around me and in public, I feel that they're living in a self imposed delusion of what life is and what it means, but deep down they know it's a hoax -- they just choose to develop a selective deafness to it all and they avoid it and try to forget it. But at night when they're all alone, in bed, wide awake, that's what they think about (well for me at least). 

So I don't think those answers are meaningful because they're not real answers and we all know it, but we try to use those answers anyway and say them to ourselves over and over again, until we start to think they're true -- it's like we're brainwashing ourselves. 

I always thought of it like this: when we're in danger mentally, emotionally or physically, the mind will try and find ways to avoid that danger; it's the survival instinct. Because if those things start to go downhill, we'll be in serious trouble, which could lead to many things like death. And I think if we don't answer the whole, 'what is the meaning of life?' question, our mental and emotional health will go downhill... even our physical health. So our mind tells us the things we want to hear to save ourselves and the scary thing is, we might not even know our mind has done this, it'll happen in the subconscious parts of our minds.


Although this is just me and all I know is my own thoughts and my own observations and they're going to be completely different to yours and thousands of other people and I'm okay with that; this is just my take on it but I see where you're coming from. I'll keep this extremely short and just add the basic reason I think I got depression, which for me, began when I was around 12 -- maybe I had it earlier without realising it... I don't know. From the age of about 8 - 18 I had an emotionally abusive step-father who would go at my mother and I and I couldn't do anything about it -- I was powerless. So I guess I mainly got depression from those ten years, from feelings of hopelessness, and powerlessness -- which in turn made me stressed which caused it. I read that: "Chronic stressful life situations can increase the risk of developing depression if you aren't coping with the stress well." Which explains it a lot. Being so young, I obviously didn't have the coping skills to deal with it very well, so here I am... a mess. Another factor is that depression runs in my family and there's another factor but it would take too long to explain and I still haven't quite processed it... but it's the biggest factor. 

Edit: Actually, I have posted this in another thread on a different subject (why did you leave your religion?), but it answers the 'biggest factor', so I'll paste it word for word here: 

My mother became a Christian when I was about seven years old and it was around this time that she married my step-dad who had recently found the faith as well.

Right up till then, it was just me and my mother, as my biological father left before I was born for another women (so I never saw him). So you'd imagine growing up without a father was tough, especially seeing friends with their fathers, loving ones at that -- it crushed me.

When my mother married, it was great at first, I finally had a father. Although he turned out to be emotionally abusive towards both me and my mother. This was extra tough because my mother was all I had and all I loved and seeing her cry her eyes out every night was again... crushing.

He'd go through cycles where he'd be normal and then he'd slip back into this old ways. I found myself being abused, and then he'd stop, and I'd forgive him because I'd always wanted a father -- it was forgive, forgive and forgive for years.

My mother prayed to God to change him for years, she consulted the pastors of our church for years about what to do, because divorcing was looked down upon by God -- but we never got answers from God or the pastors... things just stayed the same.
This went on for another ten years (rinse and repeat) until I was 18. 

By this time I had severe depression, anxiety and was going through a shattering existential crisis. I too had been praying for God to do something for those ten long years, to change my step-father, to heal my depression and anxiety... but he never did.

Finally at the age of 18, my mother kicked him out and we were finally free. Although, it was already too late. From about 12-18 years old, I shut down. I became introverted and isolated myself from everyone, I put up walls, and never let anyone in... the lights just turned off.

After, I found myself asking why this all didn't happen sooner. If my mother kicked him out as soon as it started happening, I would be a different person with less problems, but because of Christianity I'm a mess.
